name: Startup DXB
about: Founders, freelancers and small teams building in Dubai. Hiring, visas, free zones, fundraising questions and honest lessons from the trenches.

stories.author: p09
stories.text: Shipped our first paid pilot this week. Three customers, one very tired founder.

stories.author: p04
stories.text: Business Bay coworking office hours, free coffee on Wednesdays. Come say hi.

stories.author: p06
stories.text: Demo day rehearsal done. The slides are ugly but the story is clean.

posts.author: p09
posts.text: Honest question for founders: how long did your free zone licence take to set up, and was it worth it compared with a mainland company? Trying to decide before the next hiring round.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Mine took about three weeks end to end. Mainland gave more flexibility for clients in town.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Free zone is easier to start, but check which clients you can serve from it. That matters more.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Compare the total yearly cost, including the office, the visas and the renewal. Not just the licence.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Freelancer here: I started on a simple setup and upgraded later. No regrets so far.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Ask a business setup advisor for a written breakdown of fees. Keep the emails for records.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Pastry startup here, free zone worked for the kitchen lease. Good luck, Hannah!

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee roasting business, we went mainland for the wholesale clients. Depends on your model.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Swim school as a business is mainland for us. Customers come from all over the city.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's vet clinic is mainland, but the owners wanted a free zone for the lab. Mixed setups work.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: @tomasz_n three weeks is good to know. Mainland would help with local clients, I think.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: @hannah_b yes, the local client list is the deciding factor for most of us.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Also check the visa quota. Some free zones give fewer visas for the team at first.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Visa quotas are a real constraint for hiring. Ask the advisor for the exact number.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Good question. Most people underestimate the admin time, so budget for it.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Admin time is the hidden cost. A part-time accountant saves a lot of headaches.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Hire an accountant before the first invoice, it's the cheapest insurance in business.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Keep receipts and invoices organised from day one. Future you will thank you.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Yes, the accountant and the tax calendar. Put the deadlines in the team calendar.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy has no business plan but he has a lot of loyal customers. Simple model works too.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Ha, puppy has the best retention rate in the group, Mariam, honestly.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Thanks all. Going to make a comparison sheet this week and share the anonymised version.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Share the sheet in the group when it's ready. Happy to review it with you.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Yes please, a shared sheet helps everyone who is still deciding.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Good luck with the decision, Hannah. The right setup is the one that fits your clients.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Great community answers. Start small, keep records clean, and grow from there.

posts.author: p04
posts.text: Hiring lesson of the month: our best engineer came from a referral, not a job board. Build the habit of asking your network before you post a role. Free and faster.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Referrals are gold. Our last two hires were friends of friends, and both are amazing.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Ask your team for referrals with a clear job description. Vague posts don't travel well.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Good advice. A referral bonus on your first hires is a nice way to say thank you.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: As a freelancer, referrals are how I found every client. Networking is the real business.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Engineers refer engineers. Tell your team the role, and they'll tell their friends.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Our pastry team was found by a referral from a customer. Never underestimate a happy customer.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Hiring a barista through a regular customer. The trust is instant, and it's the best hire.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Swim coaches are often referred by parents. It works in every industry, apparently.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's vet nurse was a referral from a friend. Trust and care from day one.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: @hannah_b exactly. Trust is the thing you can't post in a job ad.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Also ask for referrals after a good project, not just when you're hiring. Timing matters.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: The referral programme on our team is simple: a coffee for every good introduction.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: A coffee for an introduction is a fair deal. Yusuf would approve, I'm sure.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee for introductions is my kind of incentive. Count me in for that deal.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Don't forget to thank the referrer personally. Small gestures build a strong network.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Thank-you notes work better than emails, honestly. People remember them.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: A handwritten note with a pastry box, the best thank-you I've ever given.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Good thread for the founders. Referrals, notes, and a good team culture.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy approves of the referral system. Friends bring friends, that's how a pack works.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Lovely comparison, Mariam. Yalla, the pack is growing.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Thanks all. Next post: how to write a job ad that people actually want to read.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Please do, Tomasz. Our job ads are very boring, I need help.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep the job ads short and honest. Real photos of the office help too.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Looking forward to the job ad guide. Let's make hiring less painful for everyone.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Good thread, Tomasz. Build the network first, the hiring follows.

posts.author: p07
posts.text: Pitch deck feedback request: our interior design marketplace for Dubai homes. 10 slides, no fluff. Who has seen a deck like this before and what slide would you cut first?

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Cut the team slide and merge it with the traction slide. Investors skim, so keep it short.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Your market size slide needs a bottom-up number, not just the top-down one. Investors check.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: The competition slide is the most important one for a marketplace. Show the gap clearly.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Show the customer journey with a real screenshot. A design marketplace should look good in the deck too.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Cut the roadmap if it's longer than three bullets. Nobody remembers it after the meeting.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: The before and after photos from real projects would make the deck sing. Pastry-style visuals.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Keep the ask on the last slide, clear amount and clear use of funds. Simple.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Practise the deck out loud, twice. The story has to flow without reading the slides.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy would like a slide about pets in homes, he would be the first investor.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: @mariam_s ha, a pet-friendly interior slide might be a good idea for the design brief.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Show unit economics early, even if they are rough. Founders who hide the numbers lose trust.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Agree with Hannah. A rough number with an assumption list is better than no number.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep the design slides to one visual each. Too many screenshots make the story hard to follow.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Cut the ten-item feature list down to three. Investors want the why, not the what.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: The first slide should say what you do in one sentence. Nothing else is needed there.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: A one-sentence promise on slide one, a photo of a home on slide two. Clean and warm.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee shop in a home, the design marketplace could partner with local cafes. Just an idea.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Keep the deck for a live meeting, not a long read. Send a short memo as the follow-up.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's final verdict: the slide with the dog photo gets the most attention. Use it.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Thank you all, this is incredibly useful. I'll rework the deck this week and share v2.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Send v2 when you're ready, I'll review the market slide for you.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Also rehearse the Q&A, the hardest questions come after the deck, not during.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Good luck, Anjali. A strong deck and a strong story is the best combination.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Looking forward to v2. The design marketplace is a great idea, very Dubai.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Keep the pitch short, Anjali. Five minutes and ten questions is a good rhythm.

posts.author: p01
posts.text: Working from a cafe every day is great until the wifi drops during a client call. Anyone have a reliable backup plan for Dubai? Mobile hotspot, a second SIM, something else?

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Second SIM with a data plan is my backup. Cheap, reliable, and I keep it charged in the bag.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Hotspot from the phone plus a power bank. I do a quick test before every important call.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Coworking spaces have proper internet. The day pass is cheaper than a lost client, honestly.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee shops with a good router are rare. Ask the staff which one is the most stable.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Cloud calls on a phone hotspot are fine if you mute the video. Be considerate.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: I keep a list of the stable cafes near my clients. The best coffee is the one with the wifi.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Bakery wifi is patchy, but the croissants are excellent. I plan around the croissants.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's vet clinic has the best wifi in Al Barsha, so I can join the calls from the back room.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Wired ethernet adapter for the laptop, a small investment that saves your calls.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: @hannah_b the second SIM is the cleanest backup. I'll look into it this week.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Check the coverage map of your provider before you pick the SIM. Some areas are weak.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: We keep a small coworking membership for the team, it's cheaper than the stress.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Use the coworking space for big calls and the cafe for the rest. Balance.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Good balance. Cafes are for thinking, coworking for talking, a simple rule.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Mobile hotspot with a hard limit on data, so you don't get a shock bill at month end.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Set a data alert on the plan, it's a simple thing that saves money.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: A small table near the power socket is my favourite work spot. Ask for it politely.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy can't work from a cafe, but he sits under the table and supports the calls.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Good luck with the backup plan, Sara. Calls are important, so test them first.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Thanks, everyone. Going with a second SIM and the coworking day pass for big calls.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Good combo. Keep the hotspot as the last resort, not the main plan.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Let's share a list of the cafes with good wifi in the group. Useful for everyone.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Yes, a wifi list is a great idea. Add the power socket count too, please.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Power sockets and wifi, the two things a coffee shop can offer a founder. Noted.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Good thread. Keep calm on the calls, and the wifi will follow, lol.

posts.author: p06
posts.text: Freelancers in Dubai: how do you handle late payments from clients? I have one invoice that's 60 days overdue and I'm not sure whether to send a polite reminder or a firm one.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: A polite reminder first, then a firm one with a deadline. Keep the tone professional.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Write it down in writing, every time. A phone call is fine but the email is the record.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Add a late payment clause in the next contract, it changes the conversation completely.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Ask for a deposit upfront on new projects. It filters out the clients who pay late.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Sixty days is a long time. Ask for a payment date in writing, and set a clear next step.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Bakery invoices are paid on delivery, so I can't help much here, but good luck Kwame.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Our coffee wholesale clients pay weekly now, after a few awkward months. Set the rules early.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Be firm and kind. Most late payments are simply admin forgotten, not refused.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy has no invoices, but he does have a very polite way of asking for treats. Learn from him.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Ha, puppy's negotiation skills are impressive. Thanks for the advice, everyone.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Check the contract for the payment terms, and quote them back in your reminder.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Consider a small fee for late payments if your contract allows it. Many clients respond.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep copies of the delivery proof, it helps if the dispute gets complicated.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Document everything, dates and messages. A clean paper trail is your best friend.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: If it goes on for months, a formal letter from a lawyer may be needed. Hope it doesn't come to that.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Good luck Kwame, and don't feel guilty about asking for money. You earned it.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee to clear the head before the email. Then send it calmly, and wait a day.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Sending the reminder at 9am on a weekday works better than a late-night message.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy approves of the calm and polite approach. Keep it kind, Kwame.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Thanks all, this is exactly what I needed. Reminder email going out tomorrow morning.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Let us know how it goes. The group can help with a template if you want one.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Good luck, Kwame. Keep the records and the tone professional, and you'll be fine.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Yalla, one overdue invoice at a time. Good luck, you've got this 💪

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Ask for a written payment schedule as part of the reminder, it sets a clear next step.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Keep a friendly tone in the first reminder, the client might just have forgotten.

posts.author: p02
posts.text: Build-in-public update: we went from 40 to 310 weekly active users in six weeks without a paid ad. Most came from a community post and two local newsletters. Lessons below.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Congrats, Ravi! Community first is such a clear lesson. Organic growth is the hardest and best.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Local newsletters are underrated in Dubai. Great move, and the audience is very engaged.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Six weeks to 310 is a fantastic run. What was the one post that drove the most signups?

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Build-in-public works when you show the messy parts too. Thanks for being honest.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Congratulations! The newsletter angle is worth copying for other founders in the group.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Our pastry shop got its first wave of orders from a post in a local community. Same idea!

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Community posts with a real story get the best response. Coffee and honesty go together.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Great momentum, Ravi. Keep the community close and reply to every message personally.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's community post got 40 likes. He is very proud and very ambitious.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: @anjali_rao the best post was an honest one about the first bug. People love the honesty.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Honest posts win every time. A bug story is more memorable than a feature list.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Please share the newsletter names in the group, so we can all try the same channels.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Share the lessons list too, the one you mentioned. Founders learn from each other.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Newsletters, communities and honest updates. A simple growth plan that really works.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep an eye on churn while you grow. The users who stay are the real success story.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Retention is cake and coffee for the users, keep them coming back. Simple, right?

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee and churn analysis, two words I never thought would be in the same sentence.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Good analytics are the foundation. Track the signups by channel from day one.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy approves of the community growth. The best marketing is a happy pack.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Thanks all. The lessons list is coming this week, I promise, with the numbers.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Yalla, Ravi, can't wait for the numbers. Community growth is the best kind.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Looking forward to it. Congrats again, the team should celebrate with cake.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Cake and a team dinner on the calendar. Great progress, Ravi.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Build in public, grow in public, and enjoy the ride. Congrats, Ravi 🚀

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Congratulations from the bakery team. Keep building, we're cheering from the kitchen.

posts.author: p08
posts.text: Roasting business numbers, honestly: green bean costs are up 18 percent this year, so our cup prices went up slightly. How are other food and drink founders handling price changes?

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Pastry costs are up too. We used a smaller change every quarter instead of one big jump.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Tell customers the reason, honestly. Most people accept a small change if it's explained.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Bundles and subscriptions help smooth the price changes. Loyal customers love a deal.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep the premium line and the everyday line separate. The everyday one stays steady.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Freelancer here: I raise my rates once a year and tell clients ahead of time. It works.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Sponsorship or small batch releases can help the margin too, without a big price change.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Swim school prices went up last year, and we explained the pool costs. Most families stayed.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's vet clinic had to adjust fees too. Honest explanation, same loyal customers.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Transparency with customers is the key. Share the reason and the timeline together.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: @tomasz_n that's our plan too: explain the bean market and the timeline in one note.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Ask the customers for feedback, they often suggest a better way to change prices.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: A loyalty card with a small discount, that's a nice gesture in a hard year.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Test a small price change in one location first, then scale it if it holds.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Pastry and coffee pairing deals keep the average ticket high. Great for margins.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Be careful about discounts that train customers to wait. They can hurt more than help.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Cost control on the supply side, like batch buying, is also a lever. Talk to suppliers.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Good luck, Yusuf. Hold the quality and the story, and the customers will stay.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy would be happy with any price, as long as the treats stay the same.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Ha, the puppy understands value better than most founders. Simple and true.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Thanks for the honest post, Yusuf. Founders in food need more of these conversations.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Thanks all. Next post: how we set up the wholesale price list, with the margins.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Looking forward to it. Keep the numbers simple, the group loves a clear table.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Good luck, Yusuf. A cake to go with the price change, to soften the news.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Yalla, founders, let's keep sharing the hard numbers. The group is stronger for it.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Coffee shop economics are fascinating. Thanks for the transparency, Yusuf.

posts.author: p10
posts.text: Coworking etiquette for the startup crowd: keep calls short in the open area, label your shared fridge, and please clean the coffee machine after yourself. Simple rules, big difference.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: The coffee machine rule is the most important one. Nobody likes the leftover grounds.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Shared fridge labels saved our team lunches. Add the date too, it helps.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Call booths are the best invention in a coworking space. Please use them, friends.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep your laptop charger tidy under the table, nobody wants to trip over the cables.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Freelancers in coworking spaces, we are very grateful for the simple rules. Thanks, Omar.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: A clean kitchen is a happy kitchen, the pastry team agrees completely.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee machine etiquette is my favourite topic, and yes, clean it after yourself, please.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy is not allowed in the coworking space, but the rules sound like a puppy-friendly office.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Quiet hours on the open floor would also help the focus-heavy people. Good suggestion.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Thanks all. Let's add a short rules card to the wall so the newcomers see it.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Printed rules on the wall, a simple and visible solution. Yes.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: The fridge labels will be the first thing I do on Monday. Thanks, Omar.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Good manners in a shared space are the foundation of a great community.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: A coworking community that respects the rules is a joy to work in.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Quiet calls, tidy desks, a kind neighbour. The perfect coworking life.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Pastries for the people who clean the kitchen. A small gesture to say thank you.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee for the cleaning staff is a kind idea too. Let's do it on Friday.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: A kind community, a clean desk, a happy team. Puppy approves of the whole idea.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Coworking etiquette is a small thing that makes a big difference to the mood.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Yalla, let's make the space a good place to work. Thanks for the kind replies.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Good thread, Omar. Small habits make the team better.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Share a photo of the rules card when it's up, I'll copy the design for our office.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Lovely community spirit in this thread. See you at the coworking space, friends.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Keep the rules simple, keep the coffee good, and the team will stay happy.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Coworking life with good people is the best kind. Yalla, see you on Monday 🚀

posts.author: p04
posts.text: Visa renewal season for startup teams: set the reminder 60 days before expiry, keep scans of every document, and ask your advisor for the checklist. The last-minute rush is no fun.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Sixty days is smart. We missed one renewal by a week once, it was stressful.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Scans in a shared folder with clear file names, the whole team can find things fast.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Advisor checklist is a must. Ask for the list in writing so nothing gets forgotten.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Renewal reminders in the team calendar, with an owner for each one. No orphan tasks.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Freelancers have renewals too, the same rule applies. Thanks for the clear tips, Tomasz.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: Our pastry team's visas are on a simple calendar. Visual reminders are the best.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Keep the paper copies in a folder at the office too, just in case the scans fail.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Renewal season is stressful. A shared checklist helps the whole team feel calm.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy's microchip and vaccine records are on the same kind of reminder. Very organised.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: @mariam_s yes, same discipline for pets and people. The reminder habit works for both.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Please share the checklist in the group, Tomasz. Our office will use it right away.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Yes, a shared checklist would be great. Make it one page with the dates first.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Add a note about the photos, the passport photos must be recent. Learned that the hard way.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Recent photos, clear scans, and the correct names on each document. Simple, but easy to miss.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Name spelling mistakes cause the biggest delays. Double check every letter, friends.

comments.author: p03
comments.text: A spell-check on the names, it's like the final proofing of a cake. Important.

comments.author: p08
comments.text: Coffee while you wait for the renewal confirmation, a tradition for the impatient.

comments.author: p10
comments.text: Good luck with your renewals, team. Keep calm and start early.

comments.author: p05
comments.text: Puppy wishes all the startups a smooth renewal season. He is cheering loudly.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Thanks for the great thread. Checklist coming to the group this week.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Looking forward to it. Keep the reminders going, Tomasz, the team needs them.

comments.author: p07
comments.text: Yalla, renewal season done early. A proud moment for every founder 🙌

comments.author: p01
comments.text: Good luck to everyone with the renewals. Start early and keep it boring.

comments.author: p02
comments.text: Boring is the goal for admin, and exciting for the product. Thanks, Tomasz.

comments.author: p06
comments.text: Thanks all for the advice. Let's keep the admin tidy so we can build 🚀

posts.author: p07
posts.text: Monthly startup coffee meetup at the Business Bay cafe, first Thursday at 7:30am. Founders, freelancers and anyone building something. Bring a problem, leave with an intro.

comments.author: p09
comments.text: Count me in for the first Thursday. Bringing a problem and a pastry, a good trade.

comments.author: p04
comments.text: Early start but worth it. The cafe has a quiet corner for meetings, great choice.

comments.author: p01
comments.text: A problem-and-intro format is brilliant. Very practical for a busy founder.

comments.author: p03
